title: On the Synergies between Machine Learning and Binocular Stereo for Depth Estimation from Images: a Survey
relevance_assessment: Highly relevant. The paper includes a dedicated section (Section 7) on monocular depth estimation that discusses how stereo‑supervised deep learning has enabled self‑supervised single‑image depth prediction, summarises key methods (Geometry to the Rescue, MonoDepth, AsiANet, 3Net, SuperDepth, SVS, Cross‑domain distillation, MonoResMatch, Refine & Distill, Depth‑Hints, MonoGAN, StrAT, CRF‑DGAN, PyDNet, Semi‑Supervised Monocular Depth, Semantic MonoDepth, Deep Feature Reconstruction, Monodepth2, DVSO, VOMonodepth) and presents quantitative results on KITTI (Table 6). This directly addresses the survey topic of monocular depth estimation literature up to 2025.
key_findings: Stereo‑supervised training (view synthesis loss) allows monocular networks to learn depth without ground‑truth metric labels, removing scale ambiguity present in video‑only methods.
Encoder‑decoder designs (U‑Net‑style) dominate the architecture space; multi‑task extensions (semantic segmentation, edge detection, odometry) improve accuracy.
Distillation from high‑performance stereo networks (Cross‑domain, MonoResMatch) yields dense supervision and narrows the gap to fully supervised methods.
Self‑supervised losses (photometric, left‑right consistency, minimum reprojection, auto‑masking) are crucial for handling occlusions and non‑rigid motion.
High‑resolution inputs and super‑resolution modules (SuperDepth) significantly boost depth quality, but at increased computational cost.
Lightweight models (PyDNet, MADNet‑style adaptations) enable real‑time monocular depth on CPUs/embedded devices, albeit with reduced accuracy.
Incorporating external cues (semantic hints, sparse LiDAR/VO, depth hints from classic stereo) consistently improves robustness across domains.
limitations: Generalization remains limited: performance drops on high‑resolution indoor benchmarks (Middlebury 2014) and under domain shift despite adaptation techniques.
Self‑supervised photometric losses are vulnerable to lighting changes, specularities, and moving objects, leading to artifacts in occluded regions.
Most state‑of‑the‑art models still rely on KITTI‑style outdoor scenes; few works evaluate on diverse indoor or outdoor datasets.
High‑resolution models (e.g., SuperDepth) incur high memory and runtime costs, restricting deployment on mobile platforms.
Distillation pipelines require a two‑stage training process and a strong teacher stereo network, complicating the training pipeline.
evidence_snippets: Section 7 discusses depth estimation from a single image, highlighting that “self‑supervised strategies cast depth estimation as a view‑synthesis problem by introducing a photometric reconstruction loss to avoid the need for expensive ground truth depth annotations.”

The paper lists numerous monocular methods (Geometry to the Rescue [3], MonoDepth [127], AsiANet [129], 3Net [130], SuperDepth [138], SVS [145], Cross‑domain [146], MonoResMatch [113], Refine and Distill [139], Depth‑Hints [143], MonoGAN [134], StrAT [136], CRF‑DGAN [135], PyDNet [137], Semi‑Supervised Monocular Depth [144], Semantic MonoDepth [152], Deep Feature Reconstruction [140], Monodepth2 [133], EPC++ [141], DVSO [142], VOMonodepth [148]) and their training cues (S, V, P, A, GT, etc.).
Table 6 reports quantitative KITTI results, e.g., Monodepth2 (S + V) achieving Abs Rel 0.106, RMSE log 0.193, δ < 1.25 0.876, demonstrating the effectiveness of stereo‑supervised self‑supervision.
The authors note that “current results on Middlebury 2014 highlight the open problems of generalization across different domains and applicability on high‑resolution images.”

SuperDepth achieves better accuracy by “incorporating sub‑pixel convolutional layers to super‑resolve inverse depth maps… and a differentiable flip‑augmentation layer, in order to mitigate occlusion artifacts.”
PyDNet is described as “the first attempt to make monocular depth estimation feasible on standard CPUs and embedded devices with limited memory capacity,” emphasizing real‑time constraints.

Cross‑domain distillation is summarized: “Guo et al. generate distilled depth labels, employing stereo networks trained on large synthetic datasets… Such distilled knowledge provides dense supervision for a monocular network, resulting much more effective than warping strategies.”
summary: The survey provides a comprehensive overview of monocular depth estimation up to 2025, emphasizing the pivotal role of stereo‑supervised self‑supervision. By reformulating depth prediction as view synthesis, methods such as MonoDepth and its successors eliminate the need for metric ground truth, leveraging photometric, left‑right, and minimum reprojection losses. Encoder‑decoder architectures dominate, with multi‑task extensions (semantic segmentation, edge detection, odometry) and distillation from high‑performance stereo teachers further narrowing the gap to fully supervised approaches. High‑resolution techniques (SuperDepth) boost accuracy but increase computational demands, while lightweight networks (PyDNet) enable real‑time inference on embedded hardware. Despite these advances, challenges persist: domain generalization, handling occlusions and illumination changes, and scalability to high‑resolution indoor scenes remain open problems, as highlighted by performance drops on Middlebury datasets. The paper’s detailed method catalog, quantitative KITTI benchmark (Table 6), and discussion of limitations constitute valuable evidence for a 2023‑2025 survey of monocular depth estimation.

title: Manydepth2: Motion-Aware Self-Supervised Monocular Depth Estimation in Dynamic Scenes
relevance_assessment: Highly relevant. The paper directly addresses recent advances (2023‑2025) in self‑supervised monocular depth estimation, focusing on dynamic scenes—a key challenge identified in surveys of the period. It introduces novel methodological components (pseudo‑static reference frame, motion‑aware cost volume, attention‑based HRNet) and provides extensive quantitative comparisons with state‑of‑the‑art methods on KITTI and Cityscapes.
key_findings: Manydepth2 reduces RMSE by ~5 % on KITTI‑2015 compared to similar‑cost methods, achieving the lowest Abs Rel (0.091) among listed monocular approaches.
Integrating optical flow and coarse depth to build a pseudo‑static reference frame mitigates dynamic‑object interference in the cost volume.
A motion‑aware cost volume combined with channel and non‑local attention yields a 4.1 % improvement over ManyDepth and 7.2 % over ManyDepth in Abs Rel.
On Cityscapes, Manydepth2 improves Abs Rel by ~15 % over ManyDepth, demonstrating strong performance on highly dynamic data.
Ablation studies confirm that both the motion‑guided volume and attention‑enhanced HRNet are essential for peak accuracy.
limitations: Reliance on a pretrained optical‑flow network (Gmflow) adds external dependency and slight computational overhead.
The method still assumes accurate pose estimation; errors in the pose net could affect the pseudo‑static frame construction.
Evaluations are limited to KITTI, Cityscapes, and odometry sequences; broader benchmarks (e.g., indoor or aerial) are not presented.
Dynamic‑object handling is based on flow‑derived masks, which may be unstable under severe illumination changes or motion blur.
evidence_snippets: “We utilize estimated optical flow alongside prior depth information to generate a pseudo-static reference frame. This reference frame effectively neutralizes the influence of dynamic elements within the original frame.”
“By incorporating the pseudo-static reference frame, the target frame, and the initial reference frame, we construct a novel motion-aware volume that captures the dynamics of moving objects.”
“We propose a novel depth estimation architecture that combines non-local and channel attention, enabling the integration of multi‑scale features for accurate pixel‑wise dense predictions.”
Table I shows Manydepth2 achieving Abs Rel 0.091, outperforming ManyDepth (0.098) and DynamicDepth (0.096) on KITTI‑2015.
Table II shows Manydepth2 achieving Abs Rel 0.097 on Cityscapes, a 15 % improvement over ManyDepth (0.114).
Ablation (Table V) demonstrates that removing the attention for the volume raises Abs Rel from 0.091 to 0.100, and removing motion‑guided volume raises it to 0.105.
“Manydepth2 outperforms other learning‑based techniques that use more computational resources, such as FeatDepth, reducing translational RMSE by ~24 % on KITTI odometry Seq. 10.”
summary: Manydepth2 (2025) advances self‑supervised monocular depth estimation by explicitly modeling motion in dynamic scenes. It constructs a pseudo‑static reference frame from optical flow and coarse depth, then builds a motion‑aware cost volume that feeds an attention‑enhanced HRNet decoder. Empirical results on KITTI‑2015 and Cityscapes show state‑of‑the‑art performance, with notable reductions in absolute relative error (0.091 on KITTI, 0.097 on Cityscapes) and improvements in odometry drift. Ablation studies confirm the necessity of both the motion‑guided volume and attention mechanisms. Limitations include dependence on pretrained flow networks, pose estimation sensitivity, and evaluation confined to outdoor driving datasets. Overall, the paper provides a clear, recent methodological contribution valuable for surveys covering 2023‑2025 monocular depth estimation trends.

title: MonoIndoor++: Towards Better Practice of Self-Supervised Monocular Depth Estimation for Indoor Environments
relevance_assessment: Highly relevant – the paper proposes several novel modules (depth factorization with transformer‑based scale regression, residual pose estimation, and coordinate‑convolutional encoding) that directly address challenges of indoor self‑supervised monocular depth estimation, a topic that continues to be active in 2023‑2025 surveys.
key_findings: A depth factorization module separates global depth scale (estimated via a transformer‑based scale regression network) from relative depth, improving adaptability to large indoor depth‑range variations.
A residual pose estimation module iteratively refines camera poses, mitigating large rotational motions common in handheld indoor video sequences.
Coordinate convolutional encoding (CoordConv) augments pose network inputs with explicit (x, y) image coordinates, providing additional geometric cues.
State‑of‑the‑art performance on indoor benchmarks (NYUv2, EuRoC MAV, ScanNet, 7‑Scenes), e.g., AbsRel reduced from 16.0% to 13.2% on NYUv2 and ATE improved from 0.068 m to 0.055 m on EuRoC MAV V1‑03.
Ablation studies confirm each module’s contribution: residual pose reduces AbsRel by ~1.6% on NYUv2; depth factorization adds ~0.8% gain; coordinate encoding adds further ~0.3% gain.
limitations: The method still relies on monocular video with sufficient overlap; extreme motion blur or rapid scale changes may degrade performance.
Scale regression is learned in a supervised‑like manner (probabilistic classification) and requires a maximum depth bound, limiting applicability to scenes with unknown extreme ranges.
Training complexity increases due to multiple modules (transformer, residual pose iterations, CoordConv), leading to longer training times and higher memory usage.
Evaluation is limited to a few indoor datasets; cross‑domain generalization to completely unseen indoor environments (e.g., cluttered warehouses) is not exhaustively tested.
evidence_snippets: "we propose a novel framework‑MonoIndoor++ by giving special considerations to those challenges and consolidating a set of good practices for improving the performance of self‑supervised monocular depth estimation for indoor environments"
"depth factorization module with transformer‑based scale regression network is proposed to estimate a global depth scale factor explicitly"
"residual pose estimation module to estimate relative camera poses across consecutive frames iteratively"
"coordinates convolutional encoding module... encode the coordinates information (x, y) explicitly and incorporate them with color information in the residual pose estimation module"

"Quantitative Results Table I presents the quantitative results… our model outperforms previous self‑supervised SOTA methods… reducing AbsRel from 16.0% to 13.2% and increasing δ1 from 76.7% to 83.4%"
"Table III… ATE decreased from 0.0681 m to 0.0557 m and RPE(°) reduced from 1.3237° to 0.5599°"
"Ablation results… adding our residual pose module reduces the AbsRel from 15.7% to 14.1% and increases δ1 to 81.5% on EuRoC MAV V2 01"
summary: MonoIndoor++ (2022) introduces three key innovations for self‑supervised monocular depth in indoor scenes: a depth factorization module that learns a global scale via a transformer‑based regressor, a residual pose estimator that iteratively refines camera motion to handle prevalent rotations, and coordinate‑convolutional encoding that injects explicit (x, y) cues into pose prediction. These components together achieve state‑of‑the‑art results on NYUv2, EuRoC MAV, ScanNet, and 7‑Scenes, notably cutting absolute relative error by up to 2.8% and improving pose accuracy substantially. Ablation studies validate each module's impact. Limitations include reliance on adequate video overlap, bounded scale assumptions, increased training complexity, and limited cross‑domain testing, suggesting avenues for future work in more robust, scalable indoor depth learning.
